mechanisms.description: An order whose only command revokes, vacates, restores or relinquishes is performed when it issues and is spent on issue (coordinator ruling P1); an order whose only command amends another merges into the parent on issue and its text lives or ends with the parent (ruling P2).

Relinquishment under the Act of July 5, 1884: the President places reservation lands found useless for military purposes under the Secretary of the Interior for disposal. The order ends the military reservation over the lands it names. Sec. 1 of the 1884 Act (former 43 U.S.C. 1071) was repealed on Oct. 31, 1951 (65 Stat. 706); that repeal of the authority ends no relinquishment made under it (ruling P3), and relinquishments are spent on issue in any case.

A later instrument that revokes, vacates, rescinds or supersedes the member by number or by date, or that relinquishes all of the member's lands, ends it on that instrument's date. This version uses 32 later executive orders whose texts are held, and 21 Public Land Orders whose texts are not held but whose whole-order revocation of the member is stated in BLM's official Table of Public Land Orders (held).

Members at retained bases, in the Port of Manila reservation, or that are naval reservations need the later instrument that disposed of them.

The agreement so made, the Military Bases Agreement in force March 26, 1947, retains the use of the bases listed in Annex A (and Annex B on necessity), which do not include this member's place; keeps the Port of Manila reservation (art. XXI(2)); and keeps only one other class outside the bases: 'temporary quarters and installations now existing outside the bases ... for such reasonable time, not exceeding two years', with any extension fixed by agreement, barred for the City of Manila, and one that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years' (art. XXI(1)). Member test: the reservation lies in the Philippine Islands, is an Army reservation, and its place is neither an Annex A or B base nor the Port of Manila reservation. Whether U.S. forces still occupied an installation on this member's land in 1947 is not known from the fields held; if they did, art. XXI(1) let them stay at most two years plus an extension of at most three years, so the U.S. right over the land ended no later than five years after the agreement took effect.

date_rule.basis: No later than the outer limit of art. XXI(1) of the 1947 Military Bases Agreement: two years plus an extension that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years', counted from the agreement's entry into force on 1947-03-26 (on the narrower reading that three years is the whole period, 1950-03-26; for temporary installations within the City of Manila, where no extension was allowed, 1949-03-26). July 4, 1946 (Proclamation 2695) or October 22, 1946 (Treaty art. I) for a member whose land held no U.S. installation in 1947; earlier if a later order revoked or restored the lands.

gaps: The Treaty of General Relations (61 Stat. 1174) and the Military Bases Agreement (61 Stat. 4019; 43 U.N.T.S. No. 673) are read on the web only; acquire them.

Note V of the 1947 agreement, in full: 'I have the honor to state, in signing the Agreement of March 14, 1947, Between the United States of America and the Republic of the Philippines Concerning Military Bases, the understanding of my Government that the question of the adjustment of any rights and titles held by the United States pursuant to the provisions of the Act of Congress of March 24, 1934 (48 Stat. 456) as amended, specifically Section 10(b) thereof, the Joint Resolution of the Congress of June 29, 1944, and the Act of Congress of July 3, 1946, and Treaties and Agreements heretofore entered into between the United States and the Philippines, to real property in any of the bases covered by the aforementioned Agreement or any naval reservations or fueling stations not so covered is reserved and will be settled subsequently in accordance with the terms of the Acts and Joint Resolution of the Congress mentioned above.' (61 Stat. 4033; Note VI, the Philippine reply, concurs 'without conceding the existence of any rights or titles to the real property therein referred to'.) Note V reserves title questions for the bases and for naval reservations outside them (the latter routed to B20n); it does not reserve the possession and control of an Army reservation outside the bases, which Article I surrendered. Section 5 of the 1934 Act likewise kept designated reservation lands out of the 1935 grant to the Commonwealth. Any U.S. title that outlasted the surrender is a property question disclosed here, not a continuation of the reservation.

The joint resolution of June 29, 1944 (58 Stat. 626) is read on the web only; which bases, if any, the President withheld under it before July 4, 1946 is not established in the sources held. A withheld base is retained only through the 1947 agreement, so the interval's bound covers it.

Which members' lands held U.S. temporary installations in March 1947 is not known; the interval's upper bound assumes the widest reading of art. XXI(1). A later agreement extending a temporary installation beyond the art. XXI(1) limit would be a new instrument; none is held.
